accesskeys_review_ACCESSKEY_DUPLICATE_fa: Only one of the elements responds to the key, so the others cannot be reached by their shortcut (best practice, related to WCAG 2.1.1).
accesskeys_review_ACCESSKEY_DUPLICATE_pa: Each element with that key can be reached by it, or the duplicates are intended and harmless.
accesskeys_review_ACCESSKEY_DUPLICATE_st: Note the access key the report names and find the other elements sharing it.
Press the browser's access key combination with that key (for example Alt, or Alt+Shift, plus the key) and note which element is focused or activated.
Press it again and check whether each element sharing the key can be reached.
area_altQuality_review_TEXT_ALTERNATIVE_: The text alternative is wrong, generic, a file name or doesn't say where the link leads, which fails WCAG 1.1.1 (H24).
The text alternative tells the user where the link goes, in words that match the region.
Find the image map area the report names and look at the part of the image it covers.
Click it, or follow its link, and note where it leads.
Read the area's text alternative (and every other source the report lists) and check that it says where the link leads or what the region is.
ariaAllowedAttr_review_ARIA_ATTR_DEPRECA: The state is conveyed only by the deprecated attribute and the screen reader does not announce it, so the element's state is not exposed (WCAG 4.1.2).
The state is announced, or it is also conveyed by a native attribute or a supported role, so nothing depends on the deprecated attribute alone.
Inspect the element the report names and note the deprecated aria-* attribute and the element's role.
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and check whether the attribute's state still shows on the element (for example disabled, invalid, has popup).
With a screen reader, move to the element and listen for that state being announced.
Look for a non-deprecated way to convey the same thing (a native attribute such as disabled, or a role that supports the attribute) and whether the page already uses it.
ariaAllowedRole_review_ARIA_ROLE_NOT_ALL: The announced role contradicts the element's behaviour, such as a focusable button announced as a heading, which fails ARIA in HTML and can fail WCAG 4.1.2.
The announced role matches how the element looks and behaves (or role none/presentation was ignored on a focusable control and its native role is kept).
Inspect the element the report names and note its tag and its role attribute.
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and check which role is exposed.
Press Tab to see whether the element takes keyboard focus, and try operating it with Enter or Space if it is a control.
With a screen reader, move to the element and compare what is announced with what the element does on screen.
ariaBrailleEquivalent_review_BRAILLE_ATT: A control or image has only a braille label, so speech users get no name, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
The element has a spoken name (and a roledescription where a braille one is given), or its role needs no name and nothing is lost.
Inspect the element the report names and note whether it has aria-braillelabel or aria-brailleroledescription.
If it has aria-braillelabel, open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and read the element's accessible name.
If the role is one that needs a name (button, link, image, checkbox and similar), confirm that a name exists besides the braille label; with a screen reader in speech, listen for it.
If it has aria-brailleroledescription, check whether it also has aria-roledescription; if not, confirm the native role is still announced and nothing else was meant.
ariaCheckedStateMismatch_review_ARIA_CHE: Assistive technology reports a different state from the one shown, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
The state assistive technology reports matches what the control shows, before and after it is changed.
Wait until the page has fully loaded, then find the checkbox or radio button the report names and note whether it looks checked.
Open the Accessibility pane and read its checked state.
Click it, or press Space, and check that both the look and the state in the Accessibility pane change together, or listen with a screen reader.
ariaConditionalAttr_review_ARIA_ERRORMES: Error text is visible but aria-invalid stays absent or false and the message is not announced, which fails WCAG 3.3.1 / 4.1.2 (see ARIA21).
When the error is shown, the field gets aria-invalid="true" (or the message is in aria-describedby) and the screen reader announces it; when no error is shown, nothing needs exposing.
Inspect the field the report names and note the id in its aria-errormessage.
Enter an invalid value (or leave a required field empty) and submit or leave the field, so any error appears.
Look whether the element with that id now shows error text, and inspect the field again for aria-invalid="true".
With a screen reader, move back to the field and listen for the error message.
ariaDeprecatedRole_review_ARIA_ROLE_AUTH: role="generic" strips a native meaning, such as a link or heading no longer announced as one, which fails WCAG 4.1.2 (and 1.3.1 for structure).
The element was already a generic container, or its native role still shows and is announced.
Inspect the element the report names and note its tag and role="generic".
If the tag is a plain container (div, span, b, i), the role changes nothing; remove it as cleanup.
Otherwise open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and check whether the element's native meaning (button, link, heading, list item, navigation) has been lost.
With a screen reader, move to the element and, if it is focusable, press Tab to it and listen to what is announced.
ariaDeprecatedRole_review_ARIA_ROLE_DEPR: The structure is not conveyed by assistive technology because it relies on the deprecated role, which can fail WCAG 4.1.2.
The structure is announced correctly (for example as a list with its item count), or the role is replaced with the suggested one.
Inspect the element the report names and note its deprecated role (such as directory).
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and check which role is exposed (directory is usually mapped to list).
With a screen reader, move to the element and its items and listen for the structure being announced.
Consider the suggested replacement role (list for directory) and whether it fits.
ariaExpandedStateMismatch_review_EXPANDE: The content is fully shown while the toggle tells screen reader users it is collapsed, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
The content is collapsed or only previewed while the toggle says collapsed, and the state changes when the content opens.
Find the toggle the report names; it says it is collapsed.
Look at the content it controls and check whether it is shown in full or only a preview, such as a few clamped lines.
Activate the toggle with Enter or Space and check the Accessibility pane: the expanded state should follow what is shown.
The content stays hidden while the toggle tells screen reader users it is expanded, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
The content is shown while the toggle says expanded, once any transition ends.
Find the toggle the report names; it says it is expanded.
Look for the content it controls and check whether it is shown on screen, waiting for any animation to finish.
Activate the toggle with Enter or Space and check in the Accessibility pane that the expanded state follows what is shown.
ariaHidden_focus_review_ariaHiddenFocusa: Focus reaches content behind the dialog inside aria-hidden="true", where a screen reader announces nothing, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
Focus stays inside the open dialog and never reaches the hidden content behind it.
Find the element the report names, behind the modal dialog open on the page, and note what in it can take focus.
With the dialog open, press Tab repeatedly, then Shift+Tab, and watch where focus goes.
Whenever focus seems to leave the dialog, check document.activeElement in the developer tools console.
Focus can stay on the element inside aria-hidden="true", where a screen reader announces nothing, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
Focus never stays on the hidden element: it passes straight on to a visible control, as a focus trap's sentinel does.
Click just before the element the report names, then press Tab until focus should reach it.
Watch where focus lands and check document.activeElement in the developer tools console.
Press Shift+Tab from the control after it and see whether focus stops on the hidden element or passes straight on.
ariaProhibitedAttr_review_ARIA_ATTR_PROH: The label carries information missing from the text (such as "Price in euros" on "12"), which is lost because naming is not supported on an element with no role (WCAG 4.1.2, ACT kb1m8s).
The visible text already says everything the label says, so nothing is lost if the label is ignored.
Inspect the element the report names and note its aria-label or aria-labelledby text and its visible text.
Compare the two: check whether the label says anything the visible text does not.
With a screen reader, read the element in browse mode and note whether the label is announced or ignored.
ariaRequiredAttr_review_ARIA_ATTR_REQUIR: The announced value is wrong, such as a combobox announced collapsed while its list is open or a level 2 heading that should be another level, which fails WCAG 4.1.2 (or 1.3.1 for headings).
The default value matches reality: the combobox reports collapsed only when its popup is closed, or the heading really is level 2.
Inspect the element the report names and note its role and the missing attribute (such as aria-expanded on a combobox, aria-level on a heading).
For a combobox, open and close its popup with the keyboard (Alt+Down Arrow, Escape) and the mouse, and check whether aria-expanded is added and updated.
For a heading, compare its place in the page outline with level 2, the default it gets, and check whether a different level is meant.
With a screen reader, move to the element and listen for the state or level announced.
ariaRequiredAttr_review_state_internals_: The required state is missing from the accessibility tree or does not change when the element is used, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
The state is exposed and updates as the element is used, set through its internals.
Inspect the custom element the report names and note its role and the missing state (such as checked or value).
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and check whether that state shows for the element.
Operate the element (click it, press Space or the arrow keys) and check whether the state shown in the pane changes.
With a screen reader, move to the element and listen for the state.
ariaRequiredChildren_review_ARIA_REQUIRE: It shows items (images, icons, controls) that lack the required child role, so the structure is not conveyed, which fails WCAG 1.3.1 (ACT bc4a75).
The container is empty and conveys nothing, or the items it shows carry the required role.
Inspect the container the report names and note its role and the child roles it needs (such as listitem for list, option for listbox).
Look at what it shows on screen: check whether it is empty or holds images, icons or controls.
Interact with the page (open menus, load results) and check whether children with the required role are added later.
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and check the roles of anything it holds.
ariaRoleNamePresent_review_name_internal: The element has no name in the accessibility tree and the screen reader announces only its role, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
The accessibility tree shows a name for the element, set through its internals or otherwise, and the screen reader announces it.
Inspect the custom element the report names and note its role.
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and read the element's accessible name.
With a screen reader, move to the element and listen to the name announced.
ariaRolesValid_review_ARIA_ROLE_ABSTRACT: The native role does not match the intent (such as a button marked landmark), so the meant role is never exposed, which fails WCAG 4.1.2 (ACT 674b10).
The native role is a concrete form of what the author named, so the element is still exposed correctly (still remove the abstract role).
Inspect the element the report names and note the abstract role (such as landmark, widget, command) and its tag.
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and check the role exposed instead (the native role).
Decide whether the native role is a concrete kind of the abstract role named (a nav for landmark, a button for widget).
ariaRolesValid_review_ARIA_ROLE_INVALID_: The intended role differs from the exposed one, so users get the wrong role, which fails WCAG 4.1.2 (ACT 674b10).
The exposed native role is the one that was meant, so users get the right role (still correct the typo).
Inspect the element the report names and note the unknown role value and its tag.
Work out which role was probably meant (for example "buton" for button).
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and check the role that is exposed instead (the element's native role).
Compare the exposed role with the intended one and with how the element behaves.
ariaText_review_ROLE_TEXT_HAS_FOCUSABLE_: The focusable element is announced as plain text, or not at all, so users can't tell it is interactive (best practice, WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices).
The focusable element is announced with its role and name and can be used, or it doesn't need to be focusable.
Inspect the element the report names and find the focusable element inside it.
Press Tab until that element has focus, with a screen reader running, and listen to what is announced.
Try to activate it with Enter or Space.
ariaValidAttrValue_review_ARIA_ACTIVEDES: The screen reader announces nothing or the wrong item as the active one changes, so keyboard users cannot follow it, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
Each active item is announced as the arrow keys move through it.
Inspect the element the report names and note the id in its aria-activedescendant and where that element sits.
Focus the element and use the arrow keys to move the active item.
With a screen reader running, listen whether each active item is announced as you move.
Check whether the referenced element could be moved inside the element or tied to it with aria-owns or aria-controls.
ariaValidAttrValue_review_ARIA_ATTR_VALU: The id never resolves (missing, misspelled, or across a shadow boundary), so the label, description or relation is lost, which fails WCAG 4.1.2 (ACT 6a7281).
The referenced element exists when it matters and the name, description or relation shows in the accessibility tree.
Inspect the element the report names and note the attribute and the ids it refers to.
Use the page as a user would (open, expand, submit) to reach the state where the referenced element should exist.
In the developer tools console, run document.getElementById('the-id') for each id and check for a near-miss id in the markup (different case, typo, or inside another shadow root).
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and check whether the name, description or relation it should supply appears.
ariaValidAttrValue_review_ARIA_HASPOPUP_: The popup that opens has another role than announced (such as a dialog announced as a menu), misleading screen reader users, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
The popup that opens has the role aria-haspopup announces.
Inspect the element the report names and note its aria-haspopup value (menu, listbox, tree, grid, dialog; true means menu).
Open the popup with the mouse and with the keyboard (Enter, Space or Down Arrow).
Inspect the popup that appears and check its role in the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools.
Compare the popup's role with the type aria-haspopup announces.
ariaValidAttr_review_ARIA_ATTR_INVALID_f: It is a typo of a real attribute and its effect is missing, such as a control with no name or decorative content not hidden, which fails WCAG 4.1.2 (ACT 5f99a7).
ariaValidAttr_review_ARIA_ATTR_INVALID_p: The attribute is a data hook not meant for assistive technology, or what it meant is supplied another way.
ariaValidAttr_review_ARIA_ATTR_INVALID_s: Inspect the element the report names and note the unknown aria-* attribute.
Check whether it is a misspelling of a real one (aria-lable, aria-labeledby, aria-describeby, aria-hiden) or a made-up hook (aria-qa, aria-test).
If it is a misspelling, open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and check whether what the real attribute would give (name, description, hidden state) is present anyway.
With a screen reader, move to the element and listen to what is announced.
avoidInlineSpacing_review_INLINE_SPACING: The forced value is below the metric on wrapping text and the text cannot take user spacing without loss, which fails WCAG 1.4.12.
The forced value meets the WCAG 1.4.12 metric, or the text does not wrap, or nothing is lost with the spacing applied.
Inspect the element the report names and read the !important spacing value in its style attribute.
In the Computed tab of the developer tools, read the resulting line-height, letter-spacing or word-spacing in pixels and compare with 1.5 times, 0.12 times or 0.16 times the font size.

Apply the WCAG 1.4.12 text spacing (line-height 1.5, letter-spacing 0.12em, word-spacing 0.16em, paragraph spacing 2em) with !important, for example through a user stylesheet or a bookmarklet; since the element's own !important inline style wins, also note the values it keeps.
Narrow to 320 CSS pixels and check whether the text is cut off or overlaps.
The text does wrap and, with the forced spacing, lines overlap or text is clipped, which fails WCAG 1.4.12.
The text cannot wrap (it stays on one line or scrolls) and nothing is cut off or overlaps, so the criterion does not apply.
Inspect the element the report names and note which spacing property its style attribute forces with !important.
Narrow the window to 320 CSS pixels wide (or zoom to 400%) and check whether the text ever wraps onto a second line.

Apply the WCAG 1.4.12 text spacing (line-height 1.5, letter-spacing 0.12em, word-spacing 0.16em, paragraph spacing 2em) with !important, for example through a user stylesheet or a bookmarklet; since the element's own !important inline style wins, also note the values it keeps.
Check whether any text is cut off, overlaps or is hidden.
The text wraps and the forced spacing makes lines overlap or text clip, which fails WCAG 1.4.12.
The text stays on one line at every width, or wraps without lines overlapping or text being lost.
Inspect the element the report names and note which spacing property its style attribute forces with !important.
Narrow the window to 320 CSS pixels wide (or zoom to 400%) and check whether the short text wraps onto two lines.

Apply the WCAG 1.4.12 text spacing (line-height 1.5, letter-spacing 0.12em, word-spacing 0.16em, paragraph spacing 2em) with !important, for example through a user stylesheet or a bookmarklet; since the element's own !important inline style wins, also note the values it keeps.
Check whether the text is cut off, overlaps or is hidden.
binaryControlNamePresent_review_name_int: The control has no name in the accessibility tree and the screen reader announces only its role, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
The accessibility tree shows a name for the control, set through its internals or otherwise, and the screen reader announces it.
Inspect the control the report names, a custom element, and note its role.
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and read the element's accessible name.
With a screen reader, move to the element and listen to the name announced.
buttonNamePresent_review_name_closedCont: The button has no name in the accessibility tree, since its content gives none, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
The accessibility tree shows a name for the button, taken from its content, and the screen reader announces it.
Find the button the report names and note the text or icon it shows on screen.
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and read the element's accessible name, which the browser works out from content no script can read.
With a screen reader, move to the element and listen to the name announced.
buttonNamePresent_review_name_contentToo: The button has no name in the accessibility tree, since its content gives none, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
The accessibility tree shows a name for the button, taken from its nested content, and the screen reader announces it.
Find the button the report names and note the text it shows on screen.
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and read the element's accessible name, which the browser works out from all of its nested content.
With a screen reader, move to the element and listen to the name announced.
buttonNamePresent_review_name_internals_: The button has no name in the accessibility tree and the screen reader announces only its role, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
The accessibility tree shows a name for the button, set through its internals or otherwise, and the screen reader announces it.
Inspect the button the report names, a custom element, and note its role.
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and read the element's accessible name.
With a screen reader, move to the element and listen to the name announced.
bypassBlocksPresent_review_BYPASS_MECHAN: Repeated blocks have no way to skip them, so keyboard and screen reader users must go through them on every page, which fails WCAG 2.4.1.
The page has no repeated blocks, or offers a working skip link, a main landmark or headings that let users jump past them.
Close any dialog or overlay, then look at whether the page repeats blocks such as a header or menu that appear on other pages of the site.
Click the address bar and press Tab: check whether a skip link appears that moves focus past the repeated blocks to the main content.
Check for headings at the start of the main content, or a main landmark, in the Accessibility pane or by a screen reader's headings and landmarks lists.
canvas_textAltQuality_review_TEXT_ALTERN: The text alternative is missing the information the canvas shows, or is vague or wrong, which fails WCAG 1.1.1.
The text alternative gives the same information or purpose as what the canvas shows.
Look at what the canvas the report names shows on screen, including any changes as you use it.
Read its text alternative (the value the report gives, or its fallback content and name in the Accessibility pane).
Check that the text conveys the same information or purpose as the drawing, and keeps up if the drawing changes.
clickHandlerKeyboardOperable_review_CLIC: Pressing Enter or Space does nothing even after focus arrives, which fails WCAG 2.1.1 (F54).
Enter (and Space for button-like controls) does what a click does, or, for a tab, moving focus to it already shows its panel.
Click the element the report names and note what happens.
Reload, then press Tab until the element has focus.
Press Enter, then Space, and compare with what the click did.
Pressing Enter or Space does nothing on the element, so the listener above does not handle it, which fails WCAG 2.1.1.
Enter (and Space for button-like controls) does what a click does.
Click the element the report names and note what happens.
Press Tab until the element has focus.
Press Enter, then Space (and the arrow keys if it sits in a group), and compare with the click.
The action can only be done with a mouse, which fails WCAG 2.1.1 (F54, F42).
The same action can be done by keyboard, through the managing widget or another control.
Click the element the report names and note what its click does.
Press Tab through the page and check that the element never takes focus.
If it is an item in a list, grid or combobox, focus that widget and use the arrow keys to see whether the item becomes active and Enter performs the action.
Otherwise look for another keyboard-operable control on the page that does the same thing.
No key moves focus to the element, so its action is mouse-only, which fails WCAG 2.1.1.
The element can be reached by keyboard (Tab or arrow keys within its group) and Enter or Space does what a click does.
Click the element the report names and note what happens.
Press Tab through the page and check whether focus ever lands on it.
If it is part of a group (tabs, menu, toolbar, list), Tab into the group and use the arrow keys to see whether they move focus to it.
Once it has focus, press Enter or Space and compare with the click.
Pressing Enter or Space does nothing, or less than a click, which fails WCAG 2.1.1 (F54).
Enter (and Space for button-like controls) does what a click does.
Click the element the report names and note what happens.
Reload, then press Tab until the element has focus.
Press Enter, then Space, and compare with what the click did.
comboboxNamePresent_review_name_internal: The combobox has no name in the accessibility tree and the screen reader announces only its role, which fails WCAG 4.1.2.
The accessibility tree shows a name for the combobox, set through its internals or otherwise, and the screen reader announces it.
Inspect the combobox the report names, a custom element, and note its role.
Open the Accessibility pane in the browser's developer tools and read the element's accessible name.
With a screen reader, move to the element and listen to the name announced.
contrastComputable_review_ANCESTOR_OPACI: The faded colors on screen give a ratio below the threshold, which fails WCAG 1.4.3 (or 1.4.6), unless the text is part of an inactive control.
The faded colors on screen reach the threshold, or the faded text is an inactive (disabled) control, which is exempt.
Find the text the report names and note the ancestor with opacity below 1.

Use the color picker in the browser's developer tools, or a contrast calculator with colors picked by an eyedropper, to measure the text and background as they appear on screen (faded), with an eyedropper on the rendered page.
Compare the ratio with 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text) for WCAG 1.4.3, and 7:1 (4.5:1 for large text) for 1.4.6.
contrastComputable_review_BACKGROUND_FIL: With the filter applied, the ratio on screen falls below the threshold, which fails WCAG 1.4.3 (or 1.4.6).
With the filter applied, the ratio on screen reaches the threshold.
Find the text the report names and note the filter or backdrop-filter on it or an ancestor (in the developer tools Styles pane).

Use the color picker in the browser's developer tools, or a contrast calculator with colors picked by an eyedropper, to measure the text and background colors as they appear on screen with the filter applied, using an eyedropper on the rendered page rather than the declared values.
For a blur or backdrop-filter over changing content, scroll or wait so different content passes behind, and check the worst case.
Compare the ratio with 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text) for WCAG 1.4.3, and 7:1 (4.5:1 for large text) for 1.4.6.
contrastComputable_review_BACKGROUND_IMA: Some part of the background behind the text gives a ratio below the threshold, which fails WCAG 1.4.3 (or 1.4.6).
Every part of the background behind the letters gives at least the threshold ratio.
Find the text the report names and look at the image or gradient behind it.

Use the color picker in the browser's developer tools, or a contrast calculator with colors picked by an eyedropper, to measure the text color against the lightest and darkest parts of the background directly behind the letters.
If the image changes (slides, video, responsive images), check each version and at a few window widths.
Compare the ratio with 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text) for WCAG 1.4.3, and 7:1 (4.5:1 for large text) for 1.4.6.
contrastComputable_review_BACKGROUND_NOT: The ratio is below the threshold anywhere behind the text, which fails WCAG 1.4.3 (or 1.4.6).
The ratio reaches the threshold everywhere behind the text.
Find the text the report names on the page.

Use the color picker in the browser's developer tools, or a contrast calculator with colors picked by an eyedropper, to measure the text color against the color seen directly behind the letters, taking the darkest and lightest points if it varies.
Compare the ratio with 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text) for WCAG 1.4.3, and 7:1 (4.5:1 for large text) for 1.4.6.
In some setting where the page is shown the ratio is below the threshold, which fails WCAG 1.4.3 (or 1.4.6).
The ratio reaches the threshold in every setting where the page is shown.
Find the text the report names; the page sets no opaque background behind it, so what shows there is the canvas the browser paints, or, in a frame, the page around it.
View the page where it is shown: inside the page that embeds it, with forced colors off, and in each color scheme the page supports (light and dark).
Use the color picker in the browser's developer tools, or a contrast calculator with colors picked by an eyedropper, to measure the text against the background actually seen in each setting.
Compare the ratio with 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text) for WCAG 1.4.3, and 7:1 (4.5:1 for large text) for 1.4.6.
contrastComputable_review_BACKGROUND_OVE: The color actually behind the text gives a ratio below the threshold, which fails WCAG 1.4.3 (or 1.4.6).
The color actually behind the text gives at least the threshold ratio.
Find the text the report names and check which element actually paints behind it (inspect it and toggle the overlapping element off and on).
Use the color picker in the browser's developer tools, or a contrast calculator with colors picked by an eyedropper, to measure the text color against the color actually seen behind the letters.
Compare the ratio with 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text) for WCAG 1.4.3, and 7:1 (4.5:1 for large text) for 1.4.6.
contrastComputable_review_BACKGROUND_UNP: The ratio is below the threshold, which fails WCAG 1.4.3 (or 1.4.6).
Find the text the report names and inspect the background color value in the developer tools (often a newer syntax such as oklch(), lab() or color()).
Use the color picker in the browser's developer tools, or a contrast calculator with colors picked by an eyedropper, to measure the text color against the background as rendered on screen.
Compare the ratio with 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text) for WCAG 1.4.3, and 7:1 (4.5:1 for large text) for 1.4.6.
contrastComputable_review_COLOR_SCHEME_N: In that color scheme the ratio is below the threshold, which fails WCAG 1.4.3 (or 1.4.6).
In that color scheme the ratio reaches the threshold.
Open the page in a browser set to the color scheme the report names (blockerValue: light or dark), or emulate it in the developer tools (Rendering, prefers-color-scheme).
Find the text the report names and use the color picker in the browser's developer tools, or a contrast calculator with colors picked by an eyedropper, to measure it against the background behind it.
Compare the ratio with 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text) for WCAG 1.4.3, and 7:1 (4.5:1 for large text) for 1.4.6.
contrastComputable_review_ELEMENT_OPACIT: The faded colors on screen give a ratio below the threshold, which fails WCAG 1.4.3 (or 1.4.6), unless the text is part of an inactive control.
The faded colors on screen reach the threshold, or the faded text is an inactive (disabled) control, which is exempt.
Find the text the report names and note the opacity below 1 on its element.

Use the color picker in the browser's developer tools, or a contrast calculator with colors picked by an eyedropper, to measure the text and background as they appear on screen (faded), with an eyedropper on the rendered page.
Compare the ratio with 4.5:1 (3:1 for large text) for WCAG 1.4.3, and 7:1 (4.5:1 for large text) for 1.4.6.
contrastComputable_review_ENGINE_EXCEPTI: The ratio is below the threshold for its size, which fails WCAG 1.4.3 (or 1.4.6).
The ratio reaches the threshold for its size.
Find the text the report names (the check stopped early, so nothing was measured).

passwordPasteEnabled_review_PASTE_CANCEL: Paste and password-manager filling are blocked, so the user must remember and type the value, which fails WCAG 3.3.8 unless another login method is offered.

passwordPasteEnabled_review_PASTE_HANDLE: Pasting or autofill is blocked or the value is cut or cleared, so the user must type it from memory, which fails WCAG 3.3.8 unless another login method is offered.
The pasted or autofilled value appears in full in the field.
Copy a test password or code to the clipboard.
Click in the field the report names and paste (Ctrl+V or Cmd+V, or the context menu).
Check the whole value arrives in the field (for split code boxes, across the boxes), and that no message says pasting is not allowed.
Also try filling the field with the browser's password manager.
presentationRoleConflict_review_PRESENTA: The element is meant to be hidden but its aria-* attribute or focusability brings its role back, so assistive technology exposes it anyway (best practice, WAI-ARIA presentational roles conflict resolution).

progressbarNamePresent_review_name_inter: The progress bar has no name in the accessibility tree and the screen reader announces only its role, which fails WCAG 1.1.1.

skipLink_review_SKIP_LINK_TARGET_UNUSABL: The target is hidden, not shown or has no size, so focus does not move past the repeated content (best practice, G1).
The page moves to the visible main content and the next Tab goes to the first control in it.

svg_textAltQuality_review_IMAGE_ONLY_CON: The name describes the picture, is vague, or is wrong for the action, which fails WCAG 1.1.1 (and leaves the control's purpose unclear).
The control's name says what it does or where it goes.

Activate the control and note what it does or where it goes.
Read the control's name in the Accessibility pane of the developer tools (it comes from the svg's text alternative), or Tab to it with a screen reader.

svg_textAltQuality_review_TEXT_ALTERNATI: The text alternative is wrong, vague (such as "image" or "icon") or leaves out what the graphic conveys, which fails WCAG 1.1.1.
The text alternative conveys what the graphic shows, or the decorative graphic is hidden from assistive technology.
Look at the graphic the report names and note what it shows (an icon, a logo, a chart and its data).
Read its text alternative from the report (title, desc, aria-label or aria-labelledby text), or in the Accessibility pane of the developer tools.
Compare: does the text say what the graphic shows or means? If the graphic is decorative, it should instead be hidden (aria-hidden="true").

tabindex_review_TABINDEX_POSITIVE_fail: The positive tabindex makes focus jump out of reading order, which can fail WCAG 2.4.3 (F44) and is against best practice.
tabindex_review_TABINDEX_POSITIVE_pass: Focus moves through the page in an order that matches its layout and meaning.
tabindex_review_TABINDEX_POSITIVE_step1: Click just before the start of the page, then press Tab repeatedly, watching the focus outline.
tabindex_review_TABINDEX_POSITIVE_step2: Note when the element the report names gets focus, compared with where it sits on screen.
tabindex_review_TABINDEX_POSITIVE_step3: Check whether the focus order still follows the visual and reading order of the page.
tableDuplicateName_review_TABLE_CAPTION_: The same text is read twice because caption and summary repeat each other (best practice, H39); remove the summary or make it say something else.
The table's title is announced once, and the summary (if kept) adds different information, such as how the table is laid out.
Find the table the report names and read its caption and its summary attribute in the page source.
Move to the table with a screen reader and listen to what is announced as it starts.

tableFakeCaption_review_SINGLE_CELL_FIRS: The table's title is shown only as a cell in the first row, not tied to the table as a caption, which fails WCAG 1.3.1.

Find the table the report names and look at its first row, which has one text cell.
Decide whether that cell is a title for the whole table or real data or a header for its column.
If it is a title, check in the Accessibility pane of the developer tools whether the table has a name (it should come from a caption element).
tableThHasDataCells_review_TABLE_TH_NO_A: A header that should label data has no data cells assigned to it, so its relationship is not conveyed, which fails WCAG 1.3.1.
The header is not meant to label data (it can be a plain cell), or the data it heads is marked up so the header is assigned to it.
Find the header cell the report names (its row and column are given, counting from 0).
Look at the cells below it in its column, or after it in its row, as its scope says.
Decide whether the header is meant to label data: if the cells it should head are missing, or are marked up as headers, it labels nothing.
If a screen reader is available, move through the table's data cells and note whether this header is ever announced.
tdHasHeader_review_TD_TABLE_NO_HEADERS_f: The table holds data but no cell is marked as a header, so screen reader users are not told what each value means, which fails WCAG 1.3.1 (F46).
tdHasHeader_review_TD_TABLE_NO_HEADERS_p: The table only lays out content (and should say so with role="presentation"), or its labelling cells are marked as headers.
tdHasHeader_review_TD_TABLE_NO_HEADERS_s: Look at the table the report names on screen.
Decide whether it presents data in rows and columns, with a top row or first column that labels the rest, or only lays out content side by side.
If it holds data, inspect the label row or column and check whether it uses <th> elements (or headers attributes).
textSpacingContentLoss_review_SPACING_NO: Some text is cut off, overlaps or is lost with the spacing applied, which fails WCAG 1.4.12.
All text stays visible and readable and nothing stops working with the spacing applied.

In the developer tools' Styles pane, add a new style rule for * setting line-height: 1.5 !important; letter-spacing: 0.12em !important; word-spacing: 0.16em !important, and a rule for p setting margin-bottom: 2em !important. Rules added in the Styles pane are not blocked by the page's security policy.
Scroll through the whole page and look for text that is cut off, overlaps other text or disappears.
Check that controls and menus still work and show all their text.
textSpacingContentLoss_review_STYLESHEET: The page's !important rule keeps the user's spacing from applying, which fails WCAG 1.4.12.
A user's spacing still takes effect on the element, or the content reads fine without it.
Note the rule, property and value the report gives, and find an element it styles in the Elements panel.
Add the text-spacing rules with !important in the Styles pane and check in the Computed tab whether the element's line-height, letter-spacing or word-spacing changes.
If it does not change, look at that element's text on screen with the spacing a user would apply, and check whether it stays readable.
textSpacingContentLoss_review_TEXT_CLIPP: The spacing cuts off content that cannot be reached any other way, which fails WCAG 1.4.12.
The excerpt still does its job, and the full text can be reached another way.
Find the text excerpt the report names and note how many lines it shows in full.

In the developer tools' Styles pane, add a new style rule for * setting line-height: 1.5 !important; letter-spacing: 0.12em !important; word-spacing: 0.16em !important, and a rule for p setting margin-bottom: 2em !important.
Count the lines it shows now, and check whether a 'read more' link or other way still reaches the full text.
Some of the text never appears in full with the spacing applied, which fails WCAG 1.4.12.
Every part of the moving text can still be read during its cycle.

In the developer tools' Styles pane, add a new style rule for * setting line-height: 1.5 !important; letter-spacing: 0.12em !important; word-spacing: 0.16em !important, and a rule for p setting margin-bottom: 2em !important.
Find the moving text the report names and watch it through at least one full cycle of its animation.
Pause it if there is a control, and check that all of its text can be read at some point.
Part of the text is cut off so it can no longer be read, which fails WCAG 1.4.12 (F104).
Only a sliver at the edge is cut and all the text can still be read.

In the developer tools' Styles pane, add a new style rule for * setting line-height: 1.5 !important; letter-spacing: 0.12em !important; word-spacing: 0.16em !important, and a rule for p setting margin-bottom: 2em !important.
Find the text the report names and look at the edge of the box that cuts it off.
Read the text and check whether every letter can still be made out, including the tops and tails of letters.
textSpacingContentLoss_review_TEXT_OVERL: Text is drawn over other text so that either becomes unreadable, which fails WCAG 1.4.12 (F104).
The overlap is only a sliver at the edges and both texts stay readable.

Read both and check whether either one becomes hard to read where they overlap.

videoCaption_review_CAPTIONS_REVIEW_fail: Captions are missing parts of the dialogue or important sounds, or are out of sync, which fails WCAG 1.2.2 (F8).
videoCaption_review_CAPTIONS_REVIEW_pass: The captions carry all dialogue and the important sounds, in time with the video.
videoCaption_review_CAPTIONS_REVIEW_step: Play the video the report names and turn on its captions.
Watch with the sound on and compare the captions with what is said and heard.
Check they carry all dialogue, say who is speaking when it is not clear, and describe sounds that matter (music, alarms, laughter), and that they stay in time.
videoCaption_review_CAPTIONS_TRACK_NOT_D: The video has dialogue or important sounds and no captions, which fails WCAG 1.2.2.
The video has no meaningful audio, the captions shown cover the dialogue and sounds, or it is a labelled media alternative for text on the page.
Play the video the report names with the sound on and note whether it has speech or sounds that carry information.
If it is silent or only background music with no meaning, it needs no captions.

videoCaption_review_SUBTITLES_TRACK_ONLY: The track gives the words only, with no speaker or sound information that matters, which fails WCAG 1.2.2.
The track carries the dialogue plus the speaker and sound information, so it works as captions, or the video has no audio that needs captions.

Watch with the sound on and compare the text with what is heard.
Check that besides the dialogue it says who is speaking when it is not clear and describes sounds that matter.
videoPoster_textAltPresent_review_VIDEO_: The caption does not identify the video, so the poster has no text alternative, which fails WCAG 1.1.1.

widgetKeyboardFocusable_review_ACTIVEDES: The element cannot get focus, so moving through items announces nothing or the items cannot be reached, which fails WCAG 2.1.1.
The element gets focus and the screen reader announces each active item as the arrow keys move.
Find the element the report names; it uses aria-activedescendant to point at its active item.

Press the arrow keys with a screen reader running and listen whether each active item is announced.
widgetKeyboardFocusable_review_COMPOSITE: Focus never gets into the widget or its items with the keyboard, which fails WCAG 2.1.1.
Tab (or the button that opens it) puts focus in the widget and the arrow keys move between its items.
Find the widget the report names (a menu, list box, tab list, toolbar, grid or tree).
Click just before it and press Tab, and watch whether focus enters it or one of its items.
If it is a popup, open it from its button with the keyboard and see whether focus moves into it.
Once inside, check that the arrow keys move between the items.
widgetKeyboardFocusable_review_WIDGET_NO: The widget cannot be reached or used with the keyboard and its function is not offered elsewhere, which fails WCAG 2.1.1 (F42).
The widget gets keyboard focus and works with the keyboard, or the same function is offered by another keyboard-reachable control.
Find the widget the report names and note what it does when clicked or touched.
Click just before it, then press Tab and watch whether focus ever lands on it.
If it never gets focus, look for another control a keyboard can reach that does the same thing.
If the element does nothing, its role may be wrong; note that instead.
Tab and arrow keys never reach the widget and nothing else offers its function, which fails WCAG 2.1.1.

Find the widget the report names and note when it appears (for example when a menu or dialog opens).
Use only the keyboard to open or reach that part of the page, and watch whether a script moves focus to the widget, or the arrow keys reach it.
If focus never reaches it, look for another keyboard-reachable control that does the same thing.
